newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal sector agrees wage deal in Bavaria.
newsitem.headline: German metal sector agrees wage deal in Bavaria.

text.p: Metal and engineering industry employers in the large southern German state of Bavaria said on Thursday they had reached a wage deal with the IG Metall trade union which would avert strike action.

The two sides agreed a package for some 650,000 workers. The deal did not implement cuts to sick payments that had been made possible by an unpopular new federal law and it set wages for the next two years.

The accord means 1997 wage agreements have now been signed for the majority of the 3.2 million workers in the German metal and engineering sectors, where there have been mass worker protests against the law cutting sick pay.

The Bavarian deal is similar to a breakthrough agreement reached in the northern state of Lower Saxony last Thursday, offering workers a 1.5 percent pay rise from April 1997 and a further 2.5 percent rise a year later.

Rainer Hildmann, chief negotiator for the employers, told reporters the package was "not a good agreement" as terms had largely been dictated by the Lower Saxony accord. IG Metall's Bavaria chief Werner Neugebauer called it an "acceptable compromise".

Employers in the sector have had to accept, due to the extent of worker resistance to cuts, that they will not be able to attain the sweeping labour cost reductions they had initially been hoping for in 1997.
